title: Forecasting: Time Series With ML & Foundation Models
subtitle: Why random splits lie when time matters, lag and rolling features that turn forecasting into regression, classical baselines you must beat, and the zero-shot foundation models that changed the field in 2025

objectives.title: Validate Forecasts Honestly
objectives.description: TimeSeriesSplit and rolling-origin backtests: train on the past, test on the future, never the reverse. The 4%-offline-14%-live gap has one cause.

objectives.title: Turn Forecasting Into Regression
objectives.description: Lags, rolling means, calendar features, holidays — then any regressor you already know. Gradient boosting on lag features is the workhorse of industrial demand forecasting.

objectives.title: Beat the Baselines First
objectives.description: Seasonal naive, exponential smoothing, AutoARIMA via StatsForecast. If your model can't beat 'same hour last week,' it isn't a model.

objectives.title: Use a Foundation Model Zero-Shot
objectives.description: Chronos-2 and TimesFM forecast a series they have never seen, with no training. When they win, when they don't, and how to use one as the instant baseline.

agenda.title: The Split That Sees the Future
agenda.description: Meet the data: 17,379 hours of bike rentals in Washington DC, 2011–2012, with weather and calendar. A random train/test split gives MAPE in the single digits. A time-ordered split gives triple that. The first was interpolation; only the second is forecasting.
bulletPoints: Frame it: unit = one hour, target = rentals, horizon = 24 hours ahead, decision = how many bikes to stage where
TimeSeriesSplit: expanding training window, test always later than train

agenda.title: Baselines You Must Beat
agenda.description: Naive (last value), seasonal naive (same hour last week), and a moving average. On the bike data seasonal naive lands at MAE ≈ 70 rides per hour over the last eight weeks. Everything we build tonight is judged against that number.
bulletPoints: Seasonal naive is embarrassingly hard to beat on strongly periodic data — which is most business data
Report MAE and RMSE; report MAPE only if the series never approaches zero (bikes at 4 AM do)

agenda.title: Classical Models With StatsForecast
agenda.description: Exponential smoothing (AutoETS), AutoARIMA, and Theta from Nixtla's StatsForecast — fast, well-tested, and the right second baseline. Fit on the training window, forecast the horizon, backtest with cross_validation. Then the limits: one series at a time, no weather, no holidays.
bulletPoints: StatsForecast fits AutoARIMA on thousands of series in seconds — the M5 benchmark stack
Classical models own the 'no features, short history' regime

agenda.title: Break
agenda.description: Stretch, coffee, guess tomorrow's 8 AM demand.

agenda.title: Forecasting as Regression: Lags + Gradient Boosting
agenda.description: Build features that were knowable at forecast time: rentals 24 hours ago, 168 hours ago, the 24-hour rolling mean, hour-of-day, day-of-week, holiday flag, and the weather forecast. Then HistGradientBoostingRegressor with TimeSeriesSplit. MAE drops well below the seasonal-naive baseline — and the model can use weather, which no classical model could.
bulletPoints: Every lag must respect the horizon: forecasting 24 hours ahead means the smallest usable lag is 24
mlforecast automates lags, rolling windows, and recursive multi-step forecasts for thousands of series

agenda.title: Zero-Shot: Chronos-2 and TimesFM
agenda.description: A transformer pretrained on billions of time points forecasts your series with no training at all. Chronos-2 (Amazon, Oct 2025) handles covariates and led the GIFT-Eval benchmark at release; TimesFM 2.5 (Google) is Apache-licensed. We run Chronos on the bike series and compare to the boosted model. The evidence: strong on periodic and trending series, weaker on erratic ones — and instant.
bulletPoints: Foundation models are the new first baseline: run one before you engineer a single feature
Licensing matters again: TimesFM 3.0 and TabPFN-3 weights are non-commercial; Chronos-2 is Apache-2.0

agenda.title: Wrap-Up & Project Check-In
agenda.description: The forecasting stack in 2026: seasonal naive → StatsForecast → lag features + GBM → a foundation model as the challenger, all validated with rolling-origin backtests. Project notebooks are due in 13 days.
bulletPoints: HW5 Track B is tonight's notebook with your own feature ideas, due Dec 7
Next week: neural networks, text embeddings, and LLMs as feature generators

activities.title: Beat Seasonal Naive: 24-Hour-Ahead Bike Demand
activities.description: Forecast hourly rentals one day ahead. Build the seasonal-naive baseline, then lag, rolling, and calendar features for HistGradientBoostingRegressor, validate with TimeSeriesSplit, and report MAE against the baseline — overall and by hour of day.

steps.title: Order and split by time
steps.description: Sort by datetime. Last 8 weeks are the test set; TimeSeriesSplit(5) on the rest for tuning. Never shuffle.

steps.title: Baseline
steps.description: Seasonal naive: predict the count from exactly 168 hours earlier. Compute MAE on the test weeks.

steps.title: Features knowable at forecast time
steps.description: lag_24, lag_168, rolling mean of the previous 7 days ending 24 hours ago, hour, weekday, holiday, workingday, and the weather columns (treated as the forecast).

steps.title: Model and diagnose
steps.description: HistGradientBoostingRegressor with early stopping. MAE overall, then groupby hour — where does the model still miss? Plot a test week: actual vs. baseline vs. model.

codeBlock.code:
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error

bike = pd.read_csv('hour.csv')                       # UCI Bike Sharing, hourly
bike['ts'] = pd.to_datetime(bike['dteday']) + pd.to_timedelta(bike['hr'], unit='h')
bike = bike.set_index('ts').asfreq('h')              # fill the missing hours
bike['cnt'] = bike['cnt'].interpolate()

y = bike['cnt']
feat = pd.DataFrame({
    'lag_24': y.shift(24), 'lag_168': y.shift(168),
    'roll_7d': y.shift(24).rolling(168).mean(),
    'hour': bike.index.hour, 'dow': bike.index.dayofweek,
    'holiday': bike['holiday'].ffill(), 'workingday': bike['workingday'].ffill(),
    'temp': bike['temp'].interpolate(), 'hum': bike['hum'].interpolate(), 'weathersit': bike['weathersit'].ffill(),
}).dropna()
y = y.loc[feat.index]

cut = feat.index.max() - pd.Timedelta(weeks=8)          # last 8 weeks = test
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = feat[:cut], feat[cut:], y[:cut], y[cut:]

print(f'seasonal naive MAE: {mean_absolute_error(y_te, X_te["lag_168"]):.1f} rides/hour')
gbm = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(learning_rate=0.05, max_iter=2000, early_stopping=True, random_state=835).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f'GBM MAE:            {mean_absolute_error(y_te, gbm.predict(X_te)):.1f} rides/hour  ({gbm.n_iter_} trees)')

activities.discussionNote: The boosted model beats seasonal naive by a wide margin — but look at the by-hour MAE: the biggest misses are the 8 AM and 5 PM commute peaks on days when the weather turned. That is the honest story for the operations team: we are good on normal days and we know exactly which hours to over-stage bikes on bad-weather days. Then run the optional Chronos cell: with zero features and zero training it lands between the baseline and the GBM. In 2026 that is where you start, not where you finish.

takeaways.text: Time series must be validated in time order. A random split lets lag features see the future; TimeSeriesSplit and rolling-origin backtests are the only honest scoreboards.

Forecasting is regression on features that were knowable at forecast time: lags that respect the horizon, rolling statistics, calendar, holidays, and forecast weather. Gradient boosting on those features is the industrial workhorse.
Beat seasonal naive, then StatsForecast, then run a foundation model. Chronos-2 and TimesFM forecast zero-shot and are strong on periodic series — the new instant baseline, not yet the finish line.
